brief.title: Small wheeled robot
brief.understanding: You want a robot, but haven't said yet what kind or what it should do. I've assumed a small two-wheeled rover you drive from your phone, since that is the simplest and cheapest starting point; the answers below will change the plan if you meant something else (arm, line follower, walker, etc.).

questions.question: What kind of robot do you want?
questions.why: This decides the motors, driver, frame and almost everything else.

questions.question: How should it be controlled?
questions.why: Sets which sensors and which controller are needed.

questions.question: How big should it be?
questions.why: Size sets motor power, battery size and cost.

questions.question: How should it be powered?
questions.why: Determines run time, weight and charging circuitry.

questions.question: What is your budget for parts for one robot?
questions.why: Limits the choice of motors, sensors and chassis.

requirements: Chassis about 15-20 cm long, total weight under 500 g
Two driven wheels plus one caster; top speed about 0.5 m/s on flat indoor floors
Powered by 2 x 18650 cells in series (7.4 V nominal, about 2000-2600 mAh)
Run time at least 60 minutes of continuous driving
Controlled from a phone over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, range at least 10 m indoors
Motor driver rated for at least 1 A continuous per motor
Power switch and low-battery cutoff or warning at about 6.4 V

blocks.name: Power
blocks.role: Two 18650 cells in a holder with protection and a power switch, stepped down to 3.3 V for the controller; cells are removed and charged in an external charger.
blocks.parts: 2 x protected 18650, 2S holder, 2S BMS board, 3.3 V buck regulator (e.g. MP1584 module)

blocks.name: Controller
blocks.role: Receives drive commands from the phone over Wi-Fi/Bluetooth and sets motor speed and direction.

blocks.name: Motor driver
blocks.role: Switches battery power to the two motors forward and reverse with PWM speed control.

blocks.name: Motors and wheels
blocks.role: Two geared DC motors drive the wheels; steering is done by running them at different speeds.
blocks.parts: 2 x N20 6 V metal gear motors (about 200 RPM) with 43 mm wheels, ball caster

blocks.name: Chassis
blocks.role: Holds the motors, battery and electronics.
blocks.parts: Off-the-shelf 2WD acrylic chassis kit or 3D-printed plate

risks: The idea is very open: if you meant an arm, walker or something else, the motors, driver and cost change completely. Confirm the robot type first.
Motor start-up current can dip the supply and reset the controller. Add a bulk capacitor (470 uF or more) at the driver and check the 3.3 V rail under stall.
Lithium cells can be damaged or dangerous if shorted or over-discharged. Use protected cells or a BMS, and add a fuse.
A fresh 2S pack (8.4 V) exceeds the 6 V motor rating. Limit PWM duty in firmware to keep the average voltage at or below 6 V.

product.name: Desktop two-wheeled phone-controlled rover
product.summary: A new design, so every part is assumed. A 3D-printed flat base plate (170 x 110 mm) carries two N20 gear motors with 43 mm wheels under the rear and a ball caster under the front, with a lift-off printed cover over the battery and electronics on top. Two removable protected 18650 cells in series (7.4 V nominal) feed a 2S protection board and rocker switch, then the DRV8833 motor driver directly and an MP1584 buck module for the ESP32-C3 controller, which takes drive commands from a phone over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth LE. Scale references: 18650 cells are 18 x 65 mm and the wheels are 43 mm in diameter.
product.powerInput: 2 x protected 18650 Li-ion in series, 6.0-8.4 V (7.4 V nominal), up to about 3 A peak; cells are removed for charging in an external charger

parts.name: Chassis base plate
parts.function: Flat structural plate that carries the motors and caster underneath and the battery holder, standoffs and cover on top.
parts.process: FDM 3D printing, printed flat, 4 perimeters, 40% infill
parts.evidence: Brief: 110 x 170 x 3 mm PETG plate, Z -5 to -2. Holes (not modelled as solids): M2 pairs at X +/-40, Y +55.5 and +64.5 for N20 brackets; 10 x 6 mm wire slot at X 0, Y +34; 4 M3 standoff holes at X +/-35, Y -76 and -28; 2 M3 battery holder holes at X +/-20, Y -2; 4 M3 clearance holes at X +/-50, Y +/-80 for cover screws; 2 pilot holes for the caster at X +/-12, Y -65.
parts.unknowns: Stiffness of a 3 mm flat plate over 170 mm; add ribs along the edges if it flexes under the cells.

parts.name: Lift-off top cover
parts.function: Covers the battery and electronics, and provides the USB-C, rocker switch and LED openings.
parts.process: FDM 3D printing, printed top face down so no supports are needed
parts.evidence: Brief: shell 110 x 170 mm, Z -2 to +32.5, 2 mm wall, open face down onto the plate. Openings (not modelled as solids): 13 x 8 mm USB-C cutout in the front wall at X 0, Z +8; 19 x 13 mm rocker cutout in the top at X +30, Y +29; 3 mm LED hole in the top at X -30, Y -50.
parts.unknowns: Rocker snap-in panel thickness: most 19 x 13 mm rockers want a 1 to 2 mm panel, so confirm 2 mm latches properly.

parts.name: Cover corner boss
parts.function: Printed boss in each cover corner that holds a brass heat-set insert for the cover screw.
parts.process: FDM 3D printing, integral with the cover
parts.evidence: Brief: corner bosses at X +/-50, Y +/-80. Printed as one piece with the cover; 6 x 6 mm, 8 mm tall, sitting on the plate top surface.
parts.unknowns: The rear bosses sit inside the drive team's envelope (Y 38 to 85); check they clear the motor brackets and wiring above the plate.

parts.name: M3 brass heat-set insert
parts.function: Gives the cover screws a durable metal thread in the printed bosses.
parts.process: Turned and knurled; installed with a soldering iron
parts.evidence: Brief calls for brass heat-set inserts in the corner bosses; M3 x 4 mm long, 4.6 mm OD, pressed in from the open underside of each boss.

parts.name: M3 x 8 cover screw
parts.function: Clamps the cover to the plate, entering from under the plate into the insert.
parts.package: M3 x 8 button head, hex socket
parts.evidence: Brief: 4 M3 x 8 screws at X +/-50, Y +/-80. Head sits under the plate (Z -7 to -5); the shank passes through the 3 mm plate and engages 4 to 5 mm of insert.

parts.name: Caster spacer boss
parts.function: Sets the caster height so the ball bottom reaches the floor plane at Z -32.5 and the plate rides level.
parts.evidence: Plate underside is at Z -5 and the floor at Z -32.5, a 27.5 mm drop; a 3/4 inch Pololu caster is about 23 mm tall, so a 4.5 mm spacer is needed. Printed separately or integral with the plate at X 0, Y -65.
parts.unknowns: Exact caster height varies by brand; measure it and adjust the spacer thickness so the plate is level.

parts.name: Ball caster housing
parts.function: Retains the steel ball on small rollers so the front of the rover can slide in any direction.
parts.evidence: Brief: Pololu 3/4 inch metal ball caster or equivalent. Modelled as a mounting flange with two ears plus a cup, Z -20 to -9.5.
parts.unknowns: Mounting hole spacing differs between caster brands; match the pilot holes to the part actually bought.

parts.name: Caster ball
parts.function: Third support point under the front of the rover; rolls freely in all directions.
parts.evidence: 19 mm (3/4 inch) steel ball centred at Z -23 so its bottom touches the floor at Z -32.5; only the exposed lower part (Z -32.5 to -20) is modelled, the rest sits inside the cup.

parts.name: Caster mounting screw
parts.function: Fixes the caster flange through the spacer into the plate.
parts.evidence: Two self-tapping screws from below at X +/-12, Y -65, through the flange ears and spacer into pilot holes in the plate; entered from below so nothing protrudes into the controller space above.
parts.unknowns: Screw length must not break through the plate top (3 mm plate plus 4.5 mm spacer leaves about 7 mm of plastic).

parts.name: Right N20 metal gear motor, 6 V 100:1
parts.function: Drives the right wheel at about 200 RPM no-load for differential steering.
parts.material: Steel can, brass gearbox plates, steel D shaft
parts.package: N20 micro metal gearmotor, 10 x 12 mm section
parts.evidence: Brief: N20 6 V gear motor of about 200 RPM, body X +22 to +56, 3 mm D shaft 10 mm long pointing outward on the axle line Y +60, Z -11.
parts.unknowns: Winding variant (LP, MP or HP) sets stall current, roughly 0.4 to 1.6 A at 6 V; measure stall current before finalising the driver current limit.

parts.name: Left N20 metal gear motor, 6 V 100:1
parts.function: Drives the left wheel at about 200 RPM no-load for differential steering.
parts.material: Steel can, brass gearbox plates, steel D shaft
parts.package: N20 micro metal gearmotor, 10 x 12 mm section
parts.evidence: Brief: mirror of the right motor, body X -22 to -56, shaft pointing outward.
parts.unknowns: Same as the right motor; use a matched pair so the rover tracks straight.

parts.name: 43 mm wheel, plastic hub with rubber tyre
parts.function: Converts motor rotation to traction; 43 mm diameter at 200 RPM gives about 0.45 m/s.
parts.material: ABS hub, rubber or silicone tyre
parts.process: Injection moulded hub, moulded tyre stretched on
candidates: Generic 43 mm N20 wheel, 3 mm D bore
parts.evidence: Brief: 43 x 10 mm wheel, 3 mm D-bore press fit, centred at X +/-66; the shaft tip enters the hub by 5 mm.
parts.unknowns: D-bore press-fit tightness varies by supplier; add a drop of threadlocker or a set screw if the wheel slips. In the exploded view the left copy does not move outward separately.

parts.name: N20 motor mounting bracket
parts.function: Clamps each motor can against the underside of the chassis plate.
parts.evidence: Brief: standard N20 plastic bracket at X +/-40, wrapping the 10 x 12 mm body, with two ears on 18 mm hole spacing against the plate underside at Z -5.
parts.unknowns: Hole spacing is modelled as 18 mm; measure the purchased bracket and match the plate holes to it.

parts.name: M2 x 6 pan head screw
parts.function: Fixes the bracket ears to the chassis plate.
parts.evidence: Brief: 2 M2 x 6 screws per bracket. Inserted from below; the shank passes through the 1 mm ear and the 3 mm plate and ends 2 mm above the plate top at Y 51 and Y 69, clear of the power and control boxes. This and the nut are the only drive items above Z -5.
parts.unknowns: If nothing may protrude above the plate, use hex nut pockets in the plate top and M2 x 5 screws.

parts.name: M2 hex nut
parts.function: Retains each bracket screw on the top face of the chassis plate.
parts.package: M2 hex nut, 4 mm across flats, 1.6 mm thick
parts.evidence: Brief: screws and nuts. Sits on the plate top surface at Z -2.

parts.name: 100 nF ceramic capacitor across motor terminals
parts.function: Suppresses brush noise at the source so it does not disturb the radio or reset the controller.
parts.evidence: Brief: 100 nF ceramic across each motor's terminals; soldered directly to the terminal tabs at the inboard end of each can.
parts.unknowns: The left copy sits on the left motor; in the exploded view it follows the same vector.

parts.name: Right motor lead, twisted red/black 26 AWG
parts.function: Carries the right H-bridge output from the motor driver to the right motor.
parts.material: PVC or silicone insulated stranded copper
parts.evidence: Brief: twisted pair of about 150 mm with bare tinned ends. Modelled only for the run under the plate from the terminals towards the slot at X 0, Y +34; the rest passes through the slot to the driver, outside this box.
parts.unknowns: Confirm the 150 mm length against the final driver terminal position; fix the lead to the plate underside with a dab of hot glue or a clip.

parts.name: Left motor lead, twisted red/black 26 AWG
parts.function: Carries the left H-bridge output from the motor driver to the left motor.
parts.material: PVC or silicone insulated stranded copper
parts.evidence: Brief: mirror of the right lead, about 150 mm with bare tinned ends, running to the plate slot at X 0, Y +34.
parts.unknowns: Left motor is mirrored, so swap polarity at the driver or in firmware so that forward is the same on both sides.

parts.name: 2 x 18650 series battery holder
parts.function: Holds the two removable 18650 cells side by side along X and links them in series through spring and button contacts.
parts.material: Glass-filled PP or nylon with nickel-plated steel contacts
candidates: Generic 2 x 18650 series holder with leads
parts.evidence: Brief specifies a Keystone 1049 style or generic 2S holder of about 77 x 41 x 21 mm on the plate top surface at Z -2.
parts.unknowns: Protected cells are 68-70 mm long; check that the chosen holder accepts them. A centre-tap wire must be soldered to the series link for the BMS BM pad.

parts.name: Protected 18650 Li-ion cell
parts.function: Energy source: two cells in series give 6.0-8.4 V (7.4 V nominal) at 2000-2600 mAh.
parts.evidence: Brief calls for 2 protected 18650 cells of 2000-2600 mAh lying along X in the holder.
parts.unknowns: Exact cell model and length; confirm the cell protection allows at least 3 A discharge.

parts.name: M3 x 6 countersunk screw
parts.function: Fixes the battery holder floor to the chassis plate.
parts.evidence: Brief: 2 M3 x 6 countersunk screws at X +/-20, Y -2. Only the head portion in the holder floor is modelled here; the thread continues down into the housing plate.
parts.unknowns: Whether the plate holes are tapped in plastic, use heat-set inserts or nuts below is the housing engineer's decision.

parts.name: 2S Li-ion protection board
parts.function: Hard cutoff for overcharge (8.4 V pack), over-discharge (about 5-6 V pack) and over-current or short circuit.
parts.package: Bare module with solder pads B+, BM, B-, P+, P-
parts.evidence: Brief specifies an HX-2S-JH20 style board of about 36 x 8 mm at X 0 in the strip behind the holder.
parts.unknowns: Actual over-current trip point (3-10 A depending on variant); measure or check the sense MOSFET and controller markings (typically DW01-class or S-8252 plus 8205 dual FETs).

parts.name: Double-sided foam tape pad
parts.function: Sticks the buck module and the protection board to the plate and insulates their undersides.
parts.evidence: Brief says the buck module sits on foam tape; the same pad is used under the BMS.

parts.name: MP1584EN buck module board
parts.function: Carries the step-down converter that turns switched VBAT into 3.3 V for the controller.
parts.package: 22 x 17 mm module with IN+, IN-, OUT+, OUT- pads
parts.evidence: Brief specifies an MP1584EN adjustable buck module, 22 x 17 x 4 mm overall, at X -30, trimmed to 3.3 V.
parts.unknowns: Output must be set to 3.3 V with a meter before connecting the controller; lock the trimmer with lacquer.

parts.name: MP1584EN buck regulator
parts.function: 3 A, 28 V non-synchronous step-down switcher running at about 1 MHz.
parts.evidence: Named in the brief.

parts.name: Shielded power inductor
parts.function: Energy storage for the buck converter output.
parts.evidence: Every MP1584 module carries a shielded inductor of roughly 7 x 7 mm, typically 4.7-10 uH.
parts.unknowns: Value is printed on top of the part.

parts.name: Schottky catch diode
parts.function: Freewheel path for the non-synchronous buck.
parts.evidence: The MP1584 is non-synchronous, so it needs an external Schottky.

parts.name: Output voltage trimmer
parts.function: Sets the feedback divider so the output is 3.3 V.
parts.evidence: Brief says the adjustable module is trimmed to 3.3 V.
parts.unknowns: Replacing the trimmer with fixed resistors would be more robust against vibration.

parts.name: Input and output ceramic capacitors
parts.function: Bulk decoupling on the buck input and output.
parts.evidence: Typical for the module: one 10-22 uF MLCC on each side.

parts.name: 3 A resettable polyfuse, inline
parts.function: Limits fault current in the positive lead between the protection board and the switch.
parts.package: Radial leaded PTC, 5.1 mm pitch, spliced inline
parts.evidence: Brief asks for a 3 A inline fuse or polyfuse in the positive lead; a radial PTC soldered inline under heat-shrink fits the free space below the switch.
parts.unknowns: A 3 A hold PTC trips at about 6 A, so the BMS over-current trip remains the fast protection. A 3 A mini blade fuse is an alternative if a hard fuse is preferred.

parts.name: KCD1 SPST rocker switch
parts.function: Main on/off switch in the positive lead, snapped into the cover top.
parts.evidence: Brief: KCD1 SPST rocker, 19 x 13 mm cutout, 6 A, at X +30, Y +29, body hanging down to about Z +12.
parts.unknowns: The switch stays in the cover when it is lifted off, so its two wires need about 80 mm of slack or an inline connector.

parts.name: Switched VBAT lead with 2-pin JST-XH plug
parts.function: Carries switched VBAT and ground forward along the right side of the holder to the control board.
parts.material: PVC insulated stranded copper, nylon plug housing
parts.evidence: Brief asks for a 2-pin JST-XH lead for VBAT in red/black 22 AWG running forward; routed in the 8 mm gap beside the holder.
parts.unknowns: Final length to the control board socket; leave about 40 mm beyond this box.

parts.name: 3.3 V lead with 2-pin plug
parts.function: Carries regulated 3.3 V and ground forward along the left side of the holder to the control board.
parts.material: PVC insulated stranded copper, nylon plug housing
candidates: JST PH 2-pin, so it cannot be swapped with the VBAT plug
parts.evidence: Brief asks for a 2-pin lead for 3.3 V running forward; routed in the gap on the left of the holder, next to the buck module.
parts.unknowns: Use a different connector family or keying from the VBAT lead so 8.4 V can never be plugged into the 3.3 V input.

parts.name: Carrier board 76 x 54 mm
parts.function: Carries the controller, motor driver, connectors and battery-sense parts and routes power and PWM between them.
parts.package: 4 x 3.2 mm holes at X +/-35, Y -76 / -28
parts.evidence: Brief: 76 x 54 mm, 1.6 mm FR-4 on 4 M3 standoffs, underside at Z +4.
parts.unknowns: Left motor traces run along the rear edge on the bottom layer; keep copper and ground pour out of the area under the antenna (X +/-10, Y -40 to -30).

parts.name: M3 x 6 mm nylon standoff
parts.function: Lifts the carrier board 6 mm above the base plate.
parts.evidence: Brief: 4 M3 x 6 mm nylon standoffs at X +/-35, Y -76 and Y -28; plate top at Z -2.
parts.unknowns: Screws from under the plate belong to the housing.

parts.name: M3 x 5 nylon pan-head screw
parts.function: Clamps the carrier board to the standoffs from above.
parts.evidence: Needed to hold the board on the M3 standoffs.

parts.name: Low-profile 1x15 female header (DevKit)
parts.function: Makes the ESP32-C3 dev board pluggable on the carrier.
parts.evidence: Brief: DevKitM-1 plugs into 2.54 mm female headers; two rows of 15 pins, 22.86 mm apart. Height is 3 mm socket plus 2.5 mm pin spacer.
parts.unknowns: Standard 8.5 mm sockets would raise the USB port a further 5.5 mm.

parts.name: ESP32-C3-DevKitM-1 board
parts.function: Dev board carrying the ESP32-C3 module, USB-UART bridge, 3.3 V LDO and buttons.
parts.evidence: Brief: Espressif ESP32-C3-DevKitM-1, about 39 x 25.4 mm, USB end facing -Y at X 0.
parts.unknowns: Feeding the 3V3 pin from the external buck while USB is plugged in puts two regulators in parallel on the rail. Switch the rover on while programming, or fit a Schottky/jumper; check the onboard LDO tolerates back-feed.

parts.name: ESP32-C3-MINI-1 module
parts.function: RISC-V MCU with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth LE: receives phone commands, generates 4 PWM channels, reads battery voltage.
parts.package: 13.2 x 16.6 mm LGA module with shield can
parts.evidence: Brief: DevKitM-1 uses the ESP32-C3-MINI-1 module.
parts.unknowns: Suggested pins: GPIO4-7 PWM, GPIO3 ADC, GPIO10 LED. Avoid strapping pins 2, 8, 9.

parts.name: Module PCB antenna section
parts.function: 2.4 GHz meandered trace antenna for Wi-Fi and BLE.
parts.evidence: The ESP32-C3-MINI-1 has an integral PCB antenna at the end opposite the USB port; it faces the rear here, with only low passives behind it.
parts.unknowns: Screw terminals are about 12 mm to each side, the 18650 cells about 15 mm behind. Check RSSI at 10 m; if poor, raise the dev board on taller sockets.

parts.name: Micro-USB receptacle (on DevKit)
parts.function: Programming and serial debug access.
parts.evidence: The DevKitM-1 is fitted with a Micro-USB port; it faces -Y at X 0.
parts.unknowns: With pluggable headers the port centre is at about Z +14, not Z +8 as in the brief. The housing needs a cutout about 12 x 8 mm centred at X 0, Z +14. Soldering the dev board directly only lowers it to about Z +11.

parts.name: USB-UART bridge (on DevKit)
parts.function: Converts USB to UART for flashing and logs.
parts.evidence: The DevKitM-1 carries a USB-to-UART bridge.

parts.name: Boot / Reset tact switch (on DevKit)
parts.function: Boot-mode select and reset during programming.
parts.evidence: The DevKitM-1 has BOOT and RST buttons.
parts.unknowns: Not reachable with the cover on; auto-reset through the UART bridge is normally enough.

parts.name: Low-profile 1x8 female header (driver)
parts.function: Makes the DRV8833 breakout pluggable.
parts.evidence: Brief: DRV8833 breakout on headers; Pololu #2130 has two rows of 8 pins, 10.16 mm apart.

parts.name: DRV8833 breakout board
parts.function: Carrier for the dual H-bridge with its decoupling and current-sense resistors.
parts.evidence: Brief: Pololu #2130 (20 x 13 mm). Placed rear-right, beside rather than directly behind the dev board, to keep the antenna end clear.
parts.unknowns: Pololu #2130 limits current to about 1 A per channel with its 0.2 ohm sense resistors. For 1.2 A continuous and 1.5 A peak, parallel a second 0.2 ohm on each sense pad or bridge them. Check nSLEEP is pulled high.

parts.name: DRV8833 dual H-bridge
parts.function: Drives the two N20 motors from VBAT under 20 kHz PWM on IN1-IN4.
parts.evidence: Brief names the DRV8833: 2.7-10.8 V, 1.5 A RMS per bridge.
parts.unknowns: About 0.5 W dissipated at 1.2 A in both bridges; check case temperature under the cover.

parts.name: 100 uF 16 V electrolytic
parts.function: Bulk reservoir across the driver VM pin; absorbs motor PWM ripple and start-up surges.
parts.evidence: Brief: 100 uF 16 V across VM. Placed in front of the driver, about 17 mm from the antenna.

parts.name: 2-pin screw terminal, motor outputs
parts.function: Accepts the bare tinned motor leads; left motor at X -20, right motor at X +20.
parts.evidence: Brief: two 2-pin screw terminals at the rear edge; the drive team supplies leads with bare tinned ends.
parts.unknowns: Swap the two wires of a motor if it runs backwards.

parts.name: JST-XH 2-pin header, VBAT in
parts.function: Switched battery input, 6.0-8.4 V at up to 3 A, with ground.
parts.evidence: Brief: 2-pin JST-XH input for VBAT. XH contacts are rated 3 A.
parts.unknowns: 3 A is the full XH rating; typical current is 0.6 A. Use a VH (3.96 mm) header if both motors can stall for long.

parts.name: JST-XH 2-pin header, 3.3 V in
parts.function: 3.3 V logic supply from the buck module, with ground.
parts.evidence: Brief: 2-pin JST-XH input for 3.3 V.
parts.unknowns: Identical to the VBAT header: label it, or use a 3-pin XH here so the plugs cannot be swapped.

parts.name: 100 k divider resistor
parts.function: Upper leg of the battery-sense divider from VBAT.
parts.evidence: Brief: 100 k / 33 k divider; 6.4 V x 33/133 = 1.59 V, 8.4 V gives 2.08 V.

parts.name: 33 k divider resistor
parts.function: Lower leg of the battery-sense divider to ground.
parts.evidence: Brief: 100 k / 33 k divider.

parts.name: 100 nF ADC filter capacitor
parts.function: Filters motor PWM noise at the ADC pin.
parts.evidence: Brief: 100 nF on the divider; with 24.8 k source impedance the corner is about 64 Hz.

parts.name: 330 ohm LED resistor
parts.function: Sets the LED current to about 4 mA from a 3.3 V GPIO.
parts.evidence: Brief: 330 ohm; (3.3 - 1.9) / 330 = about 4 mA.

parts.name: 3 mm red status LED
parts.function: Status light; blinks when the battery falls below 6.4 V.
parts.evidence: Brief: 3 mm red LED at X -30, Y -50 pointing up. Leads left long so the lens tip sits at Z +25.6.
parts.unknowns: Trim the lead length to suit the final height of the cover's LED hole.

connections.label: Cover rim seats on plate top (Z -2)
connections.medium: Butt joint, located by the four corner screws
connections.evidence: The cover's open face points down onto the plate; both are 110 x 170 mm.

connections.label: Integral corner bosses
connections.evidence: Bosses merge into the cover corner walls.

connections.label: Heat-set insert in boss
connections.evidence: Brief specifies brass heat-set inserts in the corner bosses.

connections.label: M3 thread, 4 places
connections.medium: Machine screw through 3.2 mm clearance hole in the plate
connections.evidence: M3 x 8: 3 mm through the plate plus 4 to 5 mm of thread engagement.

connections.label: Screw head clamps plate underside
connections.evidence: Heads sit under the plate at X +/-50, Y +/-80.

connections.label: Spacer under plate front
connections.medium: Printed integral or clamped by the caster screws
connections.evidence: 4.5 mm spacer at X 0, Y -65 sets the ride height.

connections.label: Caster flange on spacer
connections.evidence: Caster top at Z -9.5 meets the spacer bottom.

connections.label: Caster screws, 2 places
connections.evidence: Screws pass through the flange ears and spacer into the plate.

connections.label: Ball captive in cup
connections.evidence: Standard ball caster construction.

connections.label: Right motor H-bridge output
connections.medium: Soldered wire to motor terminal tabs
connections.evidence: Path sized for the continuous limit: 7.4 V at 75% duty is about 5.55 V average, 1.2 A. Typical running current is far lower, around 0.1 to 0.3 A.

connections.label: Left motor H-bridge output
connections.medium: Soldered wire to motor terminal tabs
connections.evidence: Same sizing as the right side.

connections.label: Noise suppression across right motor terminals
connections.medium: Capacitor legs soldered to the terminal tabs
connections.evidence: Brief: 100 nF across each motor; the left copy is wired the same way to the left lead.

connections.label: 3 mm D shaft press fit, right
connections.evidence: Shaft tip enters the hub by 5 mm.

connections.label: 3 mm D shaft press fit, left
connections.evidence: Left wheel is the copy at X -66.

connections.label: Bracket clamps right motor can
connections.evidence: Bracket at X +40 wraps the can.

connections.label: Bracket clamps left motor can
connections.evidence: Bracket copy at X -40.

connections.label: M2 screws through bracket ears and plate
connections.evidence: Two per bracket at Y 51 and Y 69.

connections.label: M2 nuts on plate top
connections.evidence: Nut seats on the plate top surface at Z -2.

connections.label: Pack 2S raw
connections.evidence: Two cells in series through the holder link; sized for the 3 A peak the fuse allows.

connections.label: B+
connections.evidence: Brief wiring order: holder -> BMS.

connections.label: B-
connections.evidence: Pack negative returns through the BMS protection MOSFETs.

connections.label: BM cell mid-point
connections.evidence: A 2S protection board senses each cell, so it needs a tap from the series link.

connections.label: P+ protected
connections.evidence: Brief wiring order: BMS -> fuse.

connections.label: P+ fused
connections.evidence: Brief wiring order: fuse -> switch.

connections.label: Switched VBAT
connections.evidence: Motor driver share of the 3 A fused budget at peak; about 0.6 A typical when driving.

connections.label: Switched VBAT to buck IN+
connections.evidence: 1.65 W out at about 85 percent efficiency; second wire on the switch output tab.

connections.label: VIN
connections.evidence: Module input pad to the regulator VIN pin.

connections.label: SW
connections.evidence: Switch node to inductor; 0.5 A peak load from the brief.

connections.label: 3V3
connections.medium: PCB trace, then wire from OUT+ pad
connections.evidence: Brief: 3.3 V at up to 0.5 A (about 0.15 A typical) to the controller.

connections.label: FB
connections.evidence: Feedback divider sets the 0.8 V reference point for a 3.3 V output.

connections.label: Freewheel path
connections.evidence: Catch diode conducts from ground to the switch node during the off time.

connections.label: Input and output decoupling

controls.action: Connects the battery to the motor driver and buck converter, so the controller boots, the status LED comes on and the rover waits for the phone to command the motors.

unknowns: Which cells will be used: protected 18650s are 68-70 mm long and may not fit a holder made for 65 mm cells. Measure the cells and the holder.

Two protection layers in series (protected cells plus 2S BMS): which one trips first, and whether its over-current limit allows two motors starting together (up to about 3 A). Check the BMS datasheet or test with a bench load.

The DevKit has its own 3.3 V LDO; feeding external 3.3 V into the 3V3 pin back-drives it, and plugging in USB while the battery is on puts two 3.3 V sources in parallel. Decide whether to program with the rocker off or add a diode/jumper.
Actual stall current of the chosen N20 motors at 7.4 V (often 1.0-1.6 A) against the DRV8833 current limit set by the breakout's sense resistors. Read the resistor values.
MP1584 trimmer setting: these modules ship set to arbitrary voltages. It must be set to 3.3 V before the controller is connected.
The cover has a USB-C opening but the DevKit carries micro-USB; confirm the connector type and cutout size and position.
Whether the 2.4 GHz antenna has enough clearance from the cells, wiring and motor leads for the 10 m range target; test RSSI with the cover on.
No charging path is included: cells are removed for an external charger. Confirm that is acceptable.
Motor polarity and left/right mapping at the screw terminals; settle by a drive test and swap leads or invert in firmware.
verifySteps: Before connecting the control board, power the buck module alone and adjust the trimmer to 3.30 V on the 3.3 V lead.
Measure switched VBAT at J8 with the rocker on and off (expect 6.0-8.4 V and 0 V) and check polarity of both plugs against the header silk.
Measure battery current with wheels off the ground, driving on the floor, and with both wheels stalled briefly; confirm it stays under 3 A and the BMS does not trip.
Scope the 3.3 V rail and VBAT at the driver while the motors start and reverse; look for dips that could reset the ESP32-C3.
Compare the ADC battery reading with a multimeter at 8.4, 7.4 and 6.4 V and confirm the LED blinks at 6.4 V.
Run the motors at 75% duty for 5 minutes and check the DRV8833, motors and polyfuse temperature by touch or thermocouple.
Check phone link range and RSSI with the cover fitted and motors running.
Confirm the rover sits level on both wheels and the caster and that the cover lifts off without straining the switch leads.
safety: Li-ion 18650 cells: a short can deliver tens of amps and cause fire. Never insert cells reversed, keep loose wires and tools away from the holder contacts, and remove the cells before working on the wiring.
Charge the cells only in a proper Li-ion charger, never through the rover, and do not use damaged or unwrapped cells.
The wiring between the holder and the BMS is unfused; keep it short, well insulated and clear of the screw heads and plate edges.
Do not connect USB with the rocker on unless the 3.3 V back-feed question has been resolved; it can stress the DevKit regulator or the computer's port.
A stalled motor, the driver IC and the polyfuse can get hot enough to soften a PLA print; stop driving if the rover is stuck.
Keep fingers, hair and cables away from the wheels and gearbox pinch points when powered; lift the wheels off the desk when testing firmware.
A wrongly set buck module can put up to battery voltage on the 3.3 V rail and destroy the controller; set it before connecting.

product.name: Desktop two-wheeled phone-controlled rover
product.summary: A new design, so every part is assumed. A 3D-printed flat base plate (170 x 110 mm) carries two N20 gear motors with 43 mm wheels under the rear and a ball caster under the front, with a lift-off printed cover over the battery and electronics on top. Two removable protected 18650 cells in series (7.4 V nominal) feed a 2S protection board and rocker switch, then the DRV8833 motor driver directly and an MP1584 buck module for the ESP32-C3 controller, which takes drive commands from a phone over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth LE. Scale references: 18650 cells are 18 x 65 mm and the wheels are 43 mm in diameter.
product.powerInput: 2 x protected 18650 Li-ion in series, 6.0-8.4 V (7.4 V nominal), up to about 3 A peak; cells are removed for charging in an external charger

controls.label: Power
controls.action: Connects the battery to the motor driver and buck converter, so the controller boots, the status LED comes on and the rover waits for the phone to command the motors.

unknowns: Which cells will be used: protected 18650s are 68-70 mm long and may not fit a holder made for 65 mm cells. Measure the cells and the holder.

Two protection layers in series (protected cells plus 2S BMS): which one trips first, and whether its over-current limit allows two motors starting together (up to about 3 A). Check the BMS datasheet or test with a bench load.

The DevKit has its own 3.3 V LDO; feeding external 3.3 V into the 3V3 pin back-drives it, and plugging in USB while the battery is on puts two 3.3 V sources in parallel. Decide whether to program with the rocker off or add a diode/jumper.
Actual stall current of the chosen N20 motors at 7.4 V (often 1.0-1.6 A) against the DRV8833 current limit set by the breakout's sense resistors. Read the resistor values.
MP1584 trimmer setting: these modules ship set to arbitrary voltages. It must be set to 3.3 V before the controller is connected.
The cover has a USB-C opening but the DevKit carries micro-USB; confirm the connector type and cutout size and position.
Whether the 2.4 GHz antenna has enough clearance from the cells, wiring and motor leads for the 10 m range target; test RSSI with the cover on.
No charging path is included: cells are removed for an external charger. Confirm that is acceptable.
Motor polarity and left/right mapping at the screw terminals; settle by a drive test and swap leads or invert in firmware.
verifySteps: Before connecting the control board, power the buck module alone and adjust the trimmer to 3.30 V on the 3.3 V lead.
Measure switched VBAT at J8 with the rocker on and off (expect 6.0-8.4 V and 0 V) and check polarity of both plugs against the header silk.
Measure battery current with wheels off the ground, driving on the floor, and with both wheels stalled briefly; confirm it stays under 3 A and the BMS does not trip.
Scope the 3.3 V rail and VBAT at the driver while the motors start and reverse; look for dips that could reset the ESP32-C3.
Compare the ADC battery reading with a multimeter at 8.4, 7.4 and 6.4 V and confirm the LED blinks at 6.4 V.
Run the motors at 75% duty for 5 minutes and check the DRV8833, motors and polyfuse temperature by touch or thermocouple.
Check phone link range and RSSI with the cover fitted and motors running.
Confirm the rover sits level on both wheels and the caster and that the cover lifts off without straining the switch leads.
safety: Li-ion 18650 cells: a short can deliver tens of amps and cause fire. Never insert cells reversed, keep loose wires and tools away from the holder contacts, and remove the cells before working on the wiring.
Charge the cells only in a proper Li-ion charger, never through the rover, and do not use damaged or unwrapped cells.
The wiring between the holder and the BMS is unfused; keep it short, well insulated and clear of the screw heads and plate edges.
Do not connect USB with the rocker on unless the 3.3 V back-feed question has been resolved; it can stress the DevKit regulator or the computer's port.
A stalled motor, the driver IC and the polyfuse can get hot enough to soften a PLA print; stop driving if the rover is stuck.
Keep fingers, hair and cables away from the wheels and gearbox pinch points when powered; lift the wheels off the desk when testing firmware.
A wrongly set buck module can put up to battery voltage on the 3.3 V rail and destroy the controller; set it before connecting.
